title: Milk and Honey
full_review:
"Milk & Honey" (Wellspring) is a pretentious but finely acted low-budget drama, which takes place in the course of one night, about a middle-aged Manhattan couple trying to salvage their imploding marriage, strained by suspicions of infidelity (of which they are both guilty).

Having recently recovered from a mental meltdown, stockbroker Rick Johnson (Clint Jordan) and his long-suffering wife, Joyce (Kirstin Russell) -- neither of whom is particularly likable -- host a cocktail party to reassure his colleagues (prematurely, as it turns out) that he is back to "normal." The evening ends in awkwardness and humiliation.

An ensuing tiff drives Rick on a late-night soul-searching odyssey through the streets of New York -- a la "After Hours" -- where his path intersects with that of Moses Jackson (Dudley Findlay Jr.), a fellow nighthawk with whom he strikes a macabre business deal.

Meanwhile, Joyce sets off to look for her husband but ends up in the arms -- and eventually, the bed -- of a young performance artist who reminds her of a deceased past love.

"Milk & Honey" -- with its hand-held camerawork and naturalistic performances -- echoes the films of John Cassavetes (especially "Faces," by which it was clearly inspired).

Director Joe Maggio's meditation on marital crisis illustrates how past sins can have ruinous effects on the present, but ends on a subtly hopeful note that seems to affirm the resilience of love.

"Milk & Honey" is a bit on the talky side, and the characters' behavior is undeniably reprehensible. If you don't like no-frills indie films heavy on anxiety and light on action, this one's not for you. But Maggio elicits good performances from his cast and by the end the modest movie proves somewhat satisfying, and its final image -- linked hands across a kitchen table -- says more about human frailty, remorse and reconciliation than could ever be said with words.

The film contains several instances of full-frontal or partial nudity, including one adulterous sexual encounter, brief violence and much rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
